Passage A

[1] The dune the drivers call Al-Munkhafid, forty kilometres inland from the Omani coast, will boom for you on most afternoons if you are willing to climb it. You sit near the crest, push a slab of the surface downhill with both heels, and about a second later the whole face produces a sound near 90 hertz, low enough that you feel it in the frame of your chest before you name it as a note. It lasts as long as the avalanche does. It will not do this in February, after rain.

[2] For six seasons we have measured it with geophones buried at depths from ten centimetres to two metres, and the result that organized everything else was this: the booming face is layered. The top thirty to forty centimetres are dry, loosely packed, and slower for sound; underneath sits a denser, slightly damp bed through which sound travels faster. That is the arrangement of an acoustic waveguide. Energy released at the surface cannot easily leave downward; it reflects at the boundary and runs along the dry layer, and the thickness of that layer selects which frequencies survive the round trip.

[3] The prediction that follows is unforgiving, and it is why we publish the depth profiles beside the recordings. If the layer sets the note, the note must move when the layer does. We cut a trench across one face in October and cut it again in March. The dry layer was fifty-one centimetres thick in October and twenty-nine in March; the dominant frequency rose from 76 hertz to 104. No property of the grains changed between those two visits. The grains were the same grains.

[4] We do not say the avalanche is unimportant. Without one there is no energy to guide. We say that the avalanche supplies the sound and the layer chooses the note, and that any account which locates the note in the grains alone has to explain why the same grains sang two different notes five months apart.

Passage B

[1] Sand carried out of Al-Munkhafid will boom in a laboratory chute two metres long, and that is the fact a waveguide account has to survive. There is no dune in the chute, and no six seasons of weather in it either. There is no damp bed under a dry layer; there are eight centimetres of poured sand on a steel floor, and when we shear it at the rate an avalanche shears, it gives us 95 hertz.

[2] What a shearing layer does is force grains into collisions at a common rate. Past a threshold shear rate the collisions stop being independent: a grain that strikes its neighbour a moment early is slowed, one that strikes late is driven forward, and within a few hundred collisions the whole layer is beating together. The frequency that results is fixed by the shear rate and the grain diameter, and for the grain sizes found at Al-Munkhafid it lands between 70 and 110 hertz with nobody tuning anything. We can move it where we like by shearing faster, and we have moved it across thirty hertz in a single afternoon without touching the depth of the bed.

[3] We take the trench measurement seriously and we do not think it is a mistake. We think it is ambiguous. A dune face in October and the same face in March differ in more than the thickness of a layer. They differ in how fast the avalanche runs, because the crust the avalanche has to break through weakens as the sand dries, and a thinner dry layer avalanches faster. If shear rate fixes the note, the note should climb by March, which is what was recorded. The field result agrees with both accounts, and it was collected in the one place where the two cannot be told apart.

[4] What would tell them apart is a field measurement in which layer thickness and shear rate move in opposite directions. We have not made one. Nobody has, and the reason is prosaic: the two quantities are coupled by the same drying that makes a dune boom at all. Until somebody does, the honest position is that the dune has told us its note and not its reason.

[1] The dune the drivers call Al-Munkhafid, forty kilometres inland from the Omani coast, will boom for you on most afternoons if you are willing to climb it. That is the arrangement of an acoustic waveguide. Energy released at the surface cannot easily leave downward; it reflects at the boundary and runs along the dry layer, and the thickness of that layer selects which frequencies survive the round trip.

passage:
[1] The scorebook belonged to the league and not to me, a distinction I used to find comforting. It lived in a canvas bank bag with the lineup cards and a mechanical pencil sharpened so often that the eraser end was shorter than my thumb. Every Sunday from May to August I carried the bag up the twelve steps of the press box at Rask Field, no relation, my grandmother's people spelled it with a c, and set it on the plywood shelf, and for two and a half hours the Cold Spring Millers existed in my handwriting or they did not exist at all.

[2] The job sounds clerical and is not. Balls and strikes belong to the umpire. Outs belong to the umpire. What belongs to the scorer is the small contested space between a hit and an error: whether a ball that got past a fielder got past him because the batter struck it well or because the fielder failed. The rulebook says ordinary effort. It does not say whose ordinary.

[3] My father had kept the book before me, on index cards he ruled himself with a straightedge, and he had a saying about it that I heard perhaps four hundred times: the scorer is the only person in the park who is not allowed to want anything. He meant it as instruction. I took it as description, which is how a person mistakes a wish for a fact.

[4] On the eighth of July, Ronan Petrie, who worked at the grain elevator and threw a fastball that arrived later than it looked, retired twenty-four Ellendale hitters in a row. Nobody said the word. The bench along third base had gone quiet in the fifth and stayed quiet, and by the seventh the quiet had climbed into the stands, so that the loudest thing at Rask Field was a hinge on the concession shutter.

[5] With one out in the ninth, a left-handed hitter named Boyko hit a ground ball up the middle, hard but not unplayable. Our shortstop, Marguerite Oyelaran, moved to her left, got her glove down, and the ball went under it into center field. What came out of the crowd was not a groan and not a cheer. Four hundred people ruled on the play in the same half second and then remembered that the ruling was not theirs.

[6] I looked at my hand. The pencil had already written something. This is the part I have never been able to tell straight: I do not remember choosing. I remember the shape of a 6 in the box, which is the shortstop's number, and beside it the letter E. I remember thinking that Marguerite had reached the ball, and that reaching it was the whole argument, and that my father would have said reaching is not catching. I remember that I did not look up at the press-box window, where Ronan's mother was standing, and that not looking up was itself a decision, and that I made it very deliberately, which is not what a person does who wants nothing.

[7] Ronan got the last two outs. The next morning the Herald-Sentinel ran the line score with a 0 under H and a 1 under E and the word NO-HITTER in a box, and for a week people in the IGA told me I had gotten it right, which I did not argue with, and Marguerite did not speak to me for the rest of the season, which I also did not argue with. She was twenty. She had reached a ball that ninety shortstops in a hundred do not reach, and the book said that she had failed.

[8] I gave the bag back to the league in August. I have thought since that my father's saying is true in a way he did not intend. The scorer is not allowed to want anything, not because she does not, but because the moment she admits that she does, the book stops being a record and becomes an opinion with her name on it, and everyone who reads it, herself included, has to weigh it. I had wanted Ronan to have his game. I have never been sure whether that is why I wrote what I wrote, and I no longer think the uncertainty is a failure of memory. I think it is the true part.
